core: What supervised learning is: machine learning from labeled examples that carry known answers
The two main tasks: classification (sorting into categories) and regression (predicting a number)
The supervised learning loop: study labeled examples, learn the pattern, predict labels for new cases
Where supervised learning appears: email filtering, medical diagnosis support, price prediction
Why good labels matter: labels come from human effort, and bad labels produce bad learning
supporting: Features as inputs and labels as answers (referenced; features-and-labels has its own lesson)
The human effort and cost behind creating labels
The distinction from unsupervised learning (referenced; a separate topic)
outOfScope: Unsupervised learning and clustering (own topic: unsupervised-learning)
Features and labels in depth (own topic: features-and-labels)
Training-versus-testing data splits and evaluation metrics (own topic: training-versus-testing)
Machine learning fundamentals and the ML lifecycle (own topic: machine-learning-basics)
Specific algorithms (linear regression, SVM, decision trees, neural networks)

claims.claim: Supervised learning is a machine learning approach that trains on labeled datasets, examples that pair inputs (features) with known correct outputs (labels).
Supervised learning tasks divide into two main kinds: classification, which predicts a categorical label, and regression, which predicts a numeric value.
Classification sorts cases into categories; the spam filter that predicts whether an email is spam or not is the standard example.
Regression predicts a number; examples include property selling prices, salaries, and sales revenue forecasts.

The supervised learning loop: train the model on labeled examples so it learns the relationship between features and labels, then predict labels for new, unseen cases, refining when predictions are wrong.
Labels are created by human effort, through annotation or measurement, and labeling data takes a lot of time and effort.

Supervised learning is used in email spam filtering, financial risk assessment (such as predicting loan default), medical diagnosis support (such as flagging diabetes risk from clinical metrics), and price prediction.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Logistic regression sounds like a regression task but is used for classification.
positions: Microsoft Learn notes that despite its name, logistic regression is a classification technique that predicts probabilities of class membership
IBM lists logistic regression among classification algorithms, used for binary classification such as spam identification
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson never names algorithms, so the naming trap does not surface; all three sources agree on the high-level classification-versus-regression split the lesson teaches.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How large a dataset supervised learning requires.
positions: IBM emphasizes that labeling data takes a lot of time and effort, implying label cost is the bottleneck
Google Cloud describes analyzing a large dataset of labeled training pairs
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson makes no dataset-size claims; it states only that many labeled examples are used and that labels require human effort.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether medical use of supervised learning should be described as diagnosis.
positions: Microsoft Learn frames binary classification examples such as predicting whether a patient is at risk for diabetes from clinical metrics
Google Cloud lists healthcare among the fields where supervised learning is widely used
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson carefully describes medical use as decision support, flagging patients who may be at risk so a clinician reviews, not as autonomous diagnosis.
